Name: Roope Pöyry
aboutMeContent: Lead Developer with 9 years of experience across React, .NET, and Azure. I've built multiple services from scratch, modernized older systems, and enjoy the architecture and data modeling work that makes everything downstream easier. Recently focused on integrating AI-assisted development into both my own workflow and our team's processes.

content.EasyOpp:
Designing and developing ERP software in a product development team. Two of our main applications are a mobile PWA used by our customers' employees to log, edit, and view their work hours, and a desktop web app for administrative features — approving work hours, salary calculation and transfer to integration, and the configuration of how those calculations work.

I was the main developer when we built the new mobile UI (ReactJS + TypeScript) from scratch. My responsibility was creating the foundation for further development, implementing the core features and generic components. Alongside that I reviewed other people's work and did the infrastructure setup needed for Azure deployment.

I've also been responsible for designing the renewal of our salary calculation process — both the underlying data model improvements and the related UI changes — with the goal of making the process easier and clearer for the user. A key part of the design has been considering how UI and data model changes connect, so they can be accounted for from the start of implementation.

As Senior, and now Lead Developer, I've had the opportunity to mentor junior developers, share knowledge, and help them work through different kinds of problems — feedback on which has been consistently positive. As Lead, I've also taken on broader responsibility for the product's architecture and the long-term health of the codebase.

Over the past year I've integrated Claude into both my own development workflow and our team's processes — using it for scoping, prototyping, and code review. AI-assisted development has meaningfully changed how I work, and helping the team navigate that shift has become a real part of the role.

The main technologies used have been React + TypeScript, C# + .NET, MSSQL, and Azure. I've also maintained existing E2E tests built with Robot Framework and Playwright.
content.Adalia:
Designing and developing web applications, both for customer projects across different industries and on our own Monitoring and Evaluation system.

Starting as a Junior Developer, my responsibilities grew over my time at Adalia — including mentoring new Junior Developers who joined after me. For some projects I was the sole developer responsible for maintenance, often handling multiple projects at the same time.

For one customer project I had the responsibility of starting the implementation of a completely new system from scratch: creating the application structure (React + Rails), designing the data model, and implementing user and permission management to provide a foundation for other developers to join the work.

In another project I implemented offline functionality, allowing data to be saved while the user is offline and synchronized to the server once the connection was available again. I also did my master's thesis on this specific subject, which included additional research on related topics like using service workers to cache application content in the browser.

The main technologies used were Ruby on Rails, React, and PostgreSQL. I also did configuration for services running on AWS Fargate and AWS Lambda, and worked on a Node.js API.
content.Other:
Currently building Perheraha, a family finance app for Android (Flutter, Riverpod, Drift / SQLite). The idea is to bring the family's whole financial picture — spending, net worth, accounts across multiple banks — into one place, with a low-friction monthly ritual built around CSV and PDF bank statement imports rather than manual logging. The app learns category and subscription mappings as you use it, and runs entirely on-device: no cloud, no accounts, no API keys. Currently in internal testing on Google Play, used and developed actively.

Earlier I also published Sleep Clock to the Play Store, a small utility I built as a React PWA. Side projects are how I keep learning outside my day-to-day stack — currently that means deepening Flutter and getting more hands-on with mobile development.

content.Architecture:
Designing data models and overall system architecture is the part of the work I find most rewarding — getting the foundation right is what makes everything afterward easier or harder. At EasyOpp I'm responsible for the product's architecture and codebase health, including designing the renewal of our salary calculation process, which required tightly coupling the data model changes with the user-facing flow so they could be developed together rather than retrofitted.

On the cloud side, all of our applications are hosted on Azure with deployments configured via Bicep scripts. I've worked with App Services, Azure Functions, and Table Storage, and did the Bicep setup for our React frontend running as an App Service. Earlier at Adalia I worked with AWS — setting up containerized services on Fargate with load balancers, and deploying Ruby on Jets API Gateways to AWS Lambda — which gave me a useful comparison point for how different cloud architectures work in practice.

Whether the decisions are about schema design, deployment topology, or how services talk to each other, the consistent thread is the same: thinking carefully upstream so the downstream work stays simple.
content.AIAssisted:
Over the past year I've integrated Claude into both my own development workflow and our team's processes — using it for scoping work, prototyping features, and reviewing code more thoroughly. The shift has been bigger than I expected. It's changed how I approach problem decomposition, what kinds of refactors are worth tackling, and how quickly I can ramp on unfamiliar parts of a codebase.

It also changes the discriminator between engineers. The technical work itself gets faster, so the value moves further upstream — to clearly defining what to build, recognising when a generated solution is wrong in subtle ways, and making the architectural calls that AI tools can't make for you. Helping the team navigate that shift has become a real part of the Lead Developer role for me.

My own side project Perheraha is partly a sandbox for working through these questions in practice — what AI-assisted development looks like across an entire small product, where it shines, and where it still needs careful human direction.
content.React:
I've worked with React from the start of my developer career — nine years now, in both TypeScript and JavaScript. Over that time I've designed and implemented several React applications from scratch, which has consistently been the best way for me to keep learning new things. I've also used React for personal projects, including this site and a small Android app I built as a React PWA and published to the Play Store.

I have experience with state management libraries like Redux and Redux Toolkit, and used Redux Offline for my master's thesis to provide offline functionality for users. I gravitate toward simple, reusable components and custom hooks that keep component logic clear and readable. The best thing about React is that there's always more to learn and improve on, even after this long with it.
content..NET:
I've worked with C# + .NET backends for over two years at EasyOpp, currently using mainly .NET 8 and Entity Framework Core in our APIs, with NUnit for unit tests. I've also worked with SignalR for sending real-time messages from the API to our React UI — automating much of what users would otherwise have to log manually.

Implementing the backend logic to create and update work-time entries based on vehicle location data, and then pushing those updates via SignalR, was one of the most interesting challenges I've worked on. The logic was complex with several configurable options, but the feature has held up well and needed only small tweaks since launch. The transition from Rails to .NET went smoothly, and at this point I'm comfortable developing new features effectively while still picking up new things about the framework.
content.Flutter:
Flutter is the technology I'm currently deepening on the side, building Perheraha, a family finance app for Android. The stack is Flutter with Riverpod for state management and Drift over SQLite for the local database, plus Syncfusion's pure-Dart PDF library for parsing bank statements.

What I've enjoyed most is how much of the app I've been able to design end-to-end on my own — choosing the architecture, working through migrations across schema versions, building features like CSV and PDF imports with duplicate detection, and learned-mapping rules for category and subscription matching. Mobile development has been a useful change of pace from web, and Flutter's one-codebase-for-multiple-platforms approach is genuinely elegant once you get used to the widget tree.
content.RubyOnRails:
I worked with Ruby on Rails for six years at Adalia, both maintaining existing systems and building completely new projects. I used Rails as a backend API for React frontends and as a more traditional MVC framework, set up unit tests with RSpec, and used the RSpec API Doc Generator to automate API documentation for one of the projects. I also implemented SAML authentication using Suomi.fi for a Rails + React project, allowing users to authenticate with their bank credentials.

Rails is a beginner-friendly and approachable framework, and while it's not where I'd start a new project today, I'd be happy to work with it again — there's a lot of well-earned wisdom baked into how the framework guides you toward sensible defaults.
